claim: Opioid agonists such as morphine are the gold standard for the treatment of severe pain.
source: Opioid agonists such as morphine (Figure 1; 1) are the gold standard for the treatment of severe pain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction without specific citation for this particular claim.

claim: The clinical effectiveness of opioid agonists is limited by adverse side effects that mainly result from permeation of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and activation of mu-opioid receptors in the central nervous system (CNS).
source: However, their clinical effectiveness is limited by adverse side effects that mainly result from permeation of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and activation of mu-opioid receptors in the central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Central opioid receptor activation causes sedation, apnoea, tolerance, and addiction.
source: These include sedation, apnoea, tolerance, and addiction and have recently lead to an epidemic of overdoses, death, and abuse (Kolodny et al., 2015; Passik, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kolodny et al., 2015 and Passik, 2014.

claim: Constipation due to activation of central and/or intestinal opioid receptors is a major drawback of opioid use.
source: In addition, constipation due to activation of central and/or intestinal opioid receptors is a major drawback (Schumacher et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Schumacher et al., 2015.

claim: Nonsteroidal analgesics are burdened by detrimental side effects such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcers, or cardiovascular complications.
source: and nonsteroidal analgesics are burdened by detrimental side effects such as gastrointestinal bleeding, ulcers, or cardiovascular complications (Bhala et al., 2013; Arfè et al., 2016; Sondergaard et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhala et al., 2013; Arfè et al., 2016; Sondergaard et al., 2017.

claim: Opioid receptors are expressed and functional in peripheral sensory neurons.
source: Our approach is based on opioid receptors expressed and functional in peripheral sensory neurons (Stein et al., 1990; Stein and Machelska, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stein et al., 1990 and Stein and Machelska, 2011.

claim: Opioid receptors are upregulated in injured tissue.
source: Such receptors are upregulated in injured tissue and can be targeted selectively to avoid centrally mediated side effects.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge based on the context of previous research.

claim: Local application of small, systemically inactive doses of opioid agonists has been demonstrated to potently reduce pain and inflammation in animal models and humans.
source: The local application of small, systemically inactive doses of opioid agonists has been demonstrated to potently reduce pain and inflammation in animal models and humans (Stein and Machelska, 2011; Kalso et al., 2002; Vadivelu et al., 2011; Stein et al., 1991; Stein and Küchler, 2013; Graham et al., 2013; Zeng et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: A large proportion of the analgesic effects produced by systemically administered opioids can be mediated by peripheral opioid receptors.
source: and pharmacological, genetic, and clinical studies have shown that a large proportion of the analgesic effects produced by systemically administered opioids can be mediated by peripheral opioid receptors (Labuz et al., 2007; Gaveriaux-Ruff et al., 2011; Weibel et al., 2013; Jagla et al., 2014; Stein and Jagla, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple pharmacological, genetic, and clinical studies.

claim: Peripherally restricted formulations of opioid drugs for systemic administration are not available.
source: However, peripherally restricted formulations of opioid drugs for systemic administration are not available so far.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current therapeutic options.

claim: Inflammation is accompanied by aggregation of leukocyte esterase, proteases, low pH and other mediators.
source: Inflammation is accompanied by aggregation of leukocyte esterase, proteases, low pH and other mediators
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about inflammatory processes.

claim: Inflammation is an essential component of multiple acute and chronic painful syndromes, including arthritis, endometriosis, cystitis, neuropathic pain, cancer, and surgery.
source: and is an essential component of multiple acute and chronic painful syndromes, including arthritis, endometriosis, cystitis, neuropathic pain, cancer, and surgery (Kominsky et al., 2010; Holzer, 2009; Yu et al., 2015; Rindler-Ludwig et al., 1974).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) characteristic permits diffusion of high-molecular-weight species through leaky blood vessels in inflamed tissue.
source: on the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) characteristic which permits diffusion of high-molecular-weight species through leaky blood vessels in inflamed tissue (Khandare et al., 2012; Azzopardi et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Khandare et al., 2012 and Azzopardi et al., 2013.

claim: PG-M conjugate was obtained by a two-step protocol from morphine and hyperbranched PG.
source: The PG-M conjugate (2) was obtained by a two-step protocol from morphine (1) and hyperbranched PG.
evidence: This describes the synthesis method used in the study.

claim: UV-visible spectra of dialyzed PG-M showed the absorption peak of morphine at 285 nm indicating successful immobilization of the drug on the PG scaffold.
source: UV-visible spectra of dialyzed PG-M showed the absorption peak of morphine at 285 nm indicating successful immobilization of the drug on the PG scaffold (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by UV-visible spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2.

claim: 1H-NMR revealed the characteristic appearance of proton resonance signals for morphine in the conjugated product.
source: 1H-NMR revealed the characteristic appearance of proton resonance signals for morphine in the conjugated product (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by NMR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Physical encapsulation of morphine by PG was ruled out by thin-layer chromatography (TLC) using Dragendorff and Ninhydrin as selective reagents for identifying free morphine.
source: Physical encapsulation of morphine by PG was ruled out by thin-layer chromatography (TLC) using Dragendorff and Ninhydrin as selective reagents for identifying free morphine (Figure 4)
evidence: Supported by TLC data shown in Figure 4.

claim: PG-M eluted as a single pure species with a polydispersity index (PDI) of 1.12.
source: The conjugate eluted as a single pure species (Figure 5) with a polydispersity index (PDI) of 1.12.
evidence: Supported by GPC data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The N/C ratio increased from 0.018 ± 0.01% (PG-succinate) to 7.31 ± 0.21% (PG-M), about 70-fold due to the immobilization of morphine-free base onto the PG backbone.
source: The N/C ratio increased from 0.018 ± 0.01% (PG-succinate) to 7.31 ± 0.21% (PG-M), that is, about 70-fold due to the immobilization of morphine-free base onto the PG backbone.
evidence: Supported by elemental analysis data.

claim: One unit of PG-M contained 7.31% morphine-free base.
source: One unit of PG-M contained 7.31% morphine-free base (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1.

claim: Significantly decreased pH (6.82 ± 0.02 vs. 7.20 ± 0.03; p<0.05) was found in the inflamed paw compared to controls.
source: We found significantly decreased pH (6.82 ± 0.02 vs. 7.20 ± 0.03; p<0.05, t test, N = 9)
evidence: Supported by in vivo pH measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: Dose-dependent (0–100 μg) PPT elevations (analgesia) were detected in inflamed but not in contralateral noninflamed paws after injections of morphine.
source: Dose-dependent (0–100 μg) PPT elevations (analgesia) were detected in inflamed but not in contralateral noninflamed paws after injections of morphine (Figure 6a,c)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6a,c.

claim: Dose-dependent (0–100 μg) PPT elevations (analgesia) were detected in inflamed but not in contralateral noninflamed paws after injections of PG-M.
source: Dose-dependent (0–100 μg) PPT elevations (analgesia) were detected in inflamed but not in contralateral noninflamed paws after injections of morphine (Figure 6a,c) or PG-M (Figure 6b,d).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6b,d.

claim: At a dose of 400 µg, i.pl. morphine evoked significant analgesia in both paws suggesting its systemic absorption and subsequent action in the CNS.
source: At a dose of 400 µg, i.pl. morphine evoked significant analgesia in both paws (Figure 6a,c) suggesting its systemic absorption and subsequent action in the CNS
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 6a,c with inference about mechanism.

claim: No contralateral effect was detected with the equivalent dose of PG-M (incorporating 400 µg of morphine-free base).
source: whereas no contralateral effect was detected with the equivalent dose of PG-M (incorporating 400 µg of morphine-free base) (Figure 6d).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Naloxone-methiodide (NLXM; 50 µg i.pl.) completely blocked the maximum analgesic effects in inflamed paws induced by either i.pl. morphine or PG-M.
source: Naloxone-methiodide (NLXM; 50 µg i.pl.), an opioid receptor antagonist unable to cross the BBB (Brown and Goldberg, 1985), completely blocked the maximum analgesic effects in inflamed paws induced by either i.pl. morphine or PG-M (equivalent to 100 μg morphine free base), demonstrating activation of peripheral opioid receptors by both agonists (Figure 6e,f).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 6e,f with citation to Brown and Goldberg, 1985 for NLXM properties.

claim: When the most effective dose (equivalent of 100 µg morphine free base) of PG-M was injected unilaterally into noninflamed paws, it did not alter thresholds.
source: When the most effective dose (equivalent of 100 µg morphine free base) of either compound was injected unilaterally into noninflamed paws, PG-M did not alter thresholds but morphine significantly elevated PPT in treated paws (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 2.

claim: When the most effective dose (equivalent of 100 µg morphine free base) of morphine was injected unilaterally into noninflamed paws, it significantly elevated PPT in treated paws.
source: When the most effective dose (equivalent of 100 µg morphine free base) of either compound was injected unilaterally into noninflamed paws, PG-M did not alter thresholds but morphine significantly elevated PPT in treated paws (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 2.

claim: Intravenous (i.v.) morphine produced dose-dependent analgesic effects in both inflamed and noninflamed paws.
source: Intravenous (i.v.) morphine produced dose-dependent analgesic effects in both inflamed and noninflamed paws (Figure 7a,c).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7a,c.

claim: At 12 mg/kg morphine, the cut-off PPT (250 g) was reached in both paws, accompanied by overt sedation and decreased respiratory frequency.
source: At 12 mg/kg morphine, the cut-off PPT (250 g) was reached in both paws, accompanied by overt sedation and decreased respiratory frequency.
evidence: Supported by behavioral observations in the study.

claim: I.v. PG-M (up to the equivalent of 6 mg/kg morphine-free base) produced dose-dependent analgesia selectively in inflamed paws.
source: In contrast, i.v. PG-M (up to the equivalent of 6 mg/kg morphine-free base; Table 1) produced dose-dependent analgesia selectively in inflamed paws, but did not elicit stronger effects at 12 mg/kg morphine-free base equivalent, or any changes in noninflamed paws (Figure 7b,d).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7b,d.

claim: The bilateral i.pl. injection of NLXM (50 µg/paw) did not influence the analgesic effect of 6 mg/kg i.v. morphine in noninflamed paws, and reversed the effect in inflamed paws only partially (by about half).
source: The bilateral i.pl. injection of NLXM (50 µg/paw) did not influence the analgesic effect of 6 mg/kg i.v. morphine in noninflamed paws, and reversed the effect in inflamed paws only partially (by about half), suggesting the involvement of both central and peripheral opioid receptors (Figure 7e).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7e with inference about mechanism.

claim: Analgesia induced by i.v. PG-M (equivalent to 6 mg/kg morphine free base) in inflamed paws was completely blocked by NLXM (50 µg/paw i.pl.).
source: In contrast, analgesia induced by i.v. PG-M (equivalent to 6 mg/kg morphine free base) in inflamed paws was completely blocked by NLXM (50 µg/paw i.pl.; Figure 7f), suggesting that only peripheral opioid receptors were activated.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7f with inference about mechanism.

claim: Rats receiving morphine were markedly sedated, with activity significantly lower than that of animals treated with PG-M or NaCl.
source: Rats receiving morphine were markedly sedated, similar to previous reports (Nakamura et al., 2011; Trujillo et al., 2011). Their activity was significantly lower than that of animals treated with PG-M or NaCl, while no differences between the latter two groups were detectable at any time (Figure 8a).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity data shown in Figure 8a with citations to previous reports.

claim: No differences in locomotor activity between PG-M and NaCl treated animals were detectable at any time.
source: Their activity was significantly lower than that of animals treated with PG-M or NaCl, while no differences between the latter two groups were detectable at any time (Figure 8a).
evidence: Supported by locomotor activity data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Morphine completely suppressed bowel movements.
source: Morphine completely suppressed bowel movements (similar to other studies [Nakamura et al., 2011])
evidence: Supported by constipation data with citation to Nakamura et al., 2011.

claim: Number or total weight of fecal boli were not significantly different between rats treated with PG-M or NaCl.
source: whereas number or total weight of fecal boli were not significantly different between rats treated with PG-M or NaCl (Figure 8b).
evidence: Supported by constipation data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: I.v. PG-M exclusively acts at peripheral opioid receptors in injured tissue.
source: Together, our data on analgesic, locomotor, and intestinal effects indicate that i.v. PG-M exclusively acts at peripheral opioid receptors in injured tissue.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined behavioral, locomotor, and intestinal data.

claim: I.v. morphine ubiquitously activates peripheral and central opioid receptors.
source: In contrast, i.v. morphine ubiquitously activates peripheral and central opioid receptors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined behavioral data.

claim: Up to one half of morphine's analgesic effect is mediated peripherally.
source: A rough estimate based on i.v. morphine-induced PPT elevations and their reduction by NLXM (Figure 7e) suggests that up to one half of morphine's analgesic effect is mediated peripherally, similar to studies in human patients (Jagla et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference from the data in Figure 7e with citation to Jagla et al., 2014.

claim: After unilateral i.pl. injections of morphine (equivalent to 100 µg morphine free base) into inflamed paws, up to 1200 ng/ml of morphine was detected in paw dialysates.
source: After unilateral i.pl. injections of morphine or PG-M (both equivalent to 100 µg morphine free base) into inflamed paws, we detected up to 1200 ng/ml or 576 ng/ml of morphine in paw dialysates, respectively (Figure 9a,b).
evidence: Supported by microdialysis data shown in Figure 9a.

claim: After unilateral i.pl. injections of PG-M (equivalent to 100 µg morphine free base) into inflamed paws, up to 576 ng/ml of morphine was detected in paw dialysates.
source: After unilateral i.pl. injections of morphine or PG-M (both equivalent to 100 µg morphine free base) into inflamed paws, we detected up to 1200 ng/ml or 576 ng/ml of morphine in paw dialysates, respectively (Figure 9a,b).
evidence: Supported by microdialysis data shown in Figure 9b.

claim: In contralateral noninflamed paws, morphine (about 19 ng/ml at 1 hr) was only detectable after i.pl. administration of morphine but not of PG-M.
source: In contralateral noninflamed paws, morphine (about 19 ng/ml at 1 hr) was only detectable after i.pl. administration of morphine but not of PG-M.
evidence: Supported by microdialysis data.

claim: Following 6 mg/kg i.v. morphine, mean peak morphine concentrations of up to 1700 ng/ml were measured in inflamed paws.
source: Following 6 mg/kg i.v. morphine, we measured mean peak morphine concentrations of up to 1700 ng/ml in inflamed paws (Figure 9a), 247 ng/ml in noninflamed paws, 1500 ng/ml in blood (Figure 9c), and 15 ng/ml in brain (Figure 9d).
evidence: Supported by microdialysis and tissue concentration data shown in Figures 9a, 9c, 9d.

claim: Following 6 mg/kg i.v. morphine, 247 ng/ml morphine was measured in noninflamed paws.
source: Following 6 mg/kg i.v. morphine, we measured mean peak morphine concentrations of up to 1700 ng/ml in inflamed paws (Figure 9a), 247 ng/ml in noninflamed paws, 1500 ng/ml in blood (Figure 9c), and 15 ng/ml in brain (Figure 9d).
evidence: Supported by microdialysis data.

claim: Following 6 mg/kg i.v. morphine, 1500 ng/ml morphine was measured in blood.
source: Following 6 mg/kg i.v. morphine, we measured mean peak morphine concentrations of up to 1700 ng/ml in inflamed paws (Figure 9a), 247 ng/ml in noninflamed paws, 1500 ng/ml in blood (Figure 9c), and 15 ng/ml in brain (Figure 9d).
evidence: Supported by blood concentration data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: Following 6 mg/kg i.v. morphine, 15 ng/ml morphine was measured in brain.
source: Following 6 mg/kg i.v. morphine, we measured mean peak morphine concentrations of up to 1700 ng/ml in inflamed paws (Figure 9a), 247 ng/ml in noninflamed paws, 1500 ng/ml in blood (Figure 9c), and 15 ng/ml in brain (Figure 9d).
evidence: Supported by brain concentration data shown in Figure 9d.

claim: After i.v. PG-M (equivalent to 6 mg/kg morphine-free base), up to 115 ng/ml morphine was obtained in inflamed paws.
source: After i.v. PG-M (equivalent to 6 mg/kg morphine-free base), we obtained up to 115 ng/ml morphine in inflamed paws (Figure 9b) but no relevant concentrations of free morphine in noninflamed paws (Figure 9b), blood or brain (Figure 9e) at any time.
evidence: Supported by microdialysis data shown in Figure 9b.

claim: After i.v. PG-M (equivalent to 6 mg/kg morphine-free base), no relevant concentrations of free morphine were detected in noninflamed paws, blood or brain at any time.
source: After i.v. PG-M (equivalent to 6 mg/kg morphine-free base), we obtained up to 115 ng/ml morphine in inflamed paws (Figure 9b) but no relevant concentrations of free morphine in noninflamed paws (Figure 9b), blood or brain (Figure 9e) at any time.
evidence: Supported by microdialysis and tissue concentration data shown in Figures 9b and 9e.

claim: PG-M was 10,000 times less effective than morphine to displace 4 nM [3H]-DAMGO from mu-opioid receptors.
source: In radioligand-binding studies using human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293 cells stably expressing rat mu-opioid receptors (Spahn et al., 2013), PG-M was 10,000 times less effective than morphine to displace 4 nM [3H]-([D-Ala2, N-MePhe4, Gly-ol]-enkephalin) (DAMGO), a standard mu-opioid receptor ligand.
evidence: Supported by radioligand binding assay data with citation to Spahn et al., 2013 for the cell line.

claim: PG-M does not bind to mu-opioid receptors.
source: This was demonstrated by a marked rightward shift of the concentration-response curve and a vast difference in IC50 values (Figure 10), indicating that PG-M does not bind to mu-opioid receptors.
evidence: This is an inference from the radioligand binding data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Effects on cell viability were not significantly different between morphine and PG-M, as measured by the MTT cell proliferation assay and real-time cell analysis (RTCA).
source: Effects on cell viability were not significantly different between morphine and PG-M, as measured by the MTT cell proliferation assay and real-time cell analysis (RTCA) (Figure 11).
evidence: Supported by cytotoxicity data shown in Figure 11.

claim: Separate exposure to either human leukocyte esterase (pH 7.4) or to pH 5.5 released 36% or 10%, respectively, of the initially conjugated morphine in a time-dependent manner.
source: High-performance liquid chromatography hyphenated to tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) revealed that separate exposure to either human leukocyte esterase (pH 7.4) or to pH 5.5 released 36% or 10%, respectively, of the initially conjugated morphine in a time-dependent manner (Figure 12).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 12.

claim: Chronic diseases with an inflammatory component are the greatest health threat.
source: Chronic diseases with an inflammatory component are the greatest health threat (Tabas and Glass, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tabas and Glass, 2013.

claim: Inflammation is an essential component of multiple painful syndromes such as arthritis, wounds, endometriosis, cystitis, cancer or metastatic bone pain related to osteoclasts.
source: and inflammation is an essential component of multiple painful syndromes such as arthritis, wounds, endometriosis, cystitis, cancer or metastatic bone pain related to osteoclasts (reviewed in Stein and Machelska (2011); Holzer (2009)).
evidence: Supported by citations to reviews by Stein and Machelska (2011) and Holzer (2009).

claim: Inflammation and pain can be effectively inhibited by activation of peripheral opioid receptors.
source: Since inflammation and pain can be effectively inhibited by activation of peripheral opioid receptors (Stein and Machelska, 2011; Vadivelu et al., 2011; Stein and Küchler, 2013; Zeng et al., 2013; Gaveriaux-Ruff et al., 2011; Weibel et al., 2013; Jagla et al., 2014; Spahn et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dendritic PG-based molecules are characterized by high hydrophilicity, low systemic toxicity, prolonged circulation half-life, reduced BBB permeability, and high on-target accumulation.
source: Dendritic PG-based molecules are characterized by high hydrophilicity, low systemic toxicity, prolonged circulation half-life, reduced BBB permeability, and high on-target accumulation (Baker and Carr, 2010; Khandare et al., 2012; Calderón et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baker and Carr, 2010; Khandare et al., 2012; Calderón et al., 2010.

claim: By conjugation with hydrophobic free morphine base at a low functionalization level (<10%), PG-M was expected to retain its inherent hydrophilicity.
source: By conjugation with hydrophobic free morphine base at a low functionalization level (<10%), we expected PG-M to retain its inherent hydrophilicity.
evidence: This is a design hypothesis stated by the authors.

claim: PG-M released morphine when exposed to either leukocyte esterase or acidic pH in vitro.
source: This compound released morphine when exposed to either leukocyte esterase or acidic pH in vitro.
evidence: Supported by in vitro release data.

claim: Polymer conjugates can selectively aggregate in tumor tissue based on the EPR effect.
source: Because polymer conjugates can selectively aggregate in tumor tissue based on the EPR effect (Khandare et al., 2012; Azzopardi et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Khandare et al., 2012 and Azzopardi et al., 2013.

claim: The hyperpermeable vasculature in inflamed tissue would permit a targeted accumulation of PG-M and subsequent release of free morphine in vivo.
source: we assumed that the hyperpermeable vasculature in inflamed tissue would permit a targeted accumulation of PG-M and subsequent release of free morphine in vivo.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors.

claim: Both conventional morphine and PG-M produced stronger analgesic effects in inflamed than in noninflamed tissue.
source: Using a standard model of high predictive validity for clinical analgesia (Stein and Machelska, 2011; Kalso et al., 2002; Stein et al., 1991; Stein, 1993; Machelska et al., 1998; Le Bars et al., 2001; Whiteside et al., 2008), we found that both conventional morphine and PG-M produced stronger analgesic effects in inflamed than in noninflamed tissue.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data with citations to previous studies validating the model.

claim: The stronger analgesic effects in inflamed tissue have been attributed to upregulation, increased functionality and accessibility of peripheral opioid receptors.
source: This is consistent with numerous experimental and clinical studies and has been attributed to upregulation, increased functionality and accessibility of peripheral opioid receptors (Stein and Machelska, 2011; Kalso et al., 2002; Spahn et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: After local injection of conventional morphine or PG-M into inflamed paws, peak morphine concentrations in microdialysates coincided with peak analgesic effects within 5–20 min.
source: After local injection of conventional morphine or PG-M into inflamed paws, peak morphine concentrations in microdialysates coincided with peak analgesic effects within 5–20 min.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined behavioral and microdialysis data.

claim: Peak morphine concentrations in microdialysates were about twice as high after conventional morphine than after PG-M, even though the same absolute amounts of morphine were administered.
source: These concentrations were about twice as high after conventional morphine than after PG-M, even though we administered the same absolute amounts of morphine.
evidence: This is an observation from the microdialysis data.

claim: The lower morphine concentrations after PG-M may be due to protracted release of morphine from the conjugate.
source: This may be due to protracted release of morphine from the conjugate.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Maximum efficacy is determined by the available number of peripheral opioid receptors rather than by the amount of agonist.
source: The effects of both compounds were of similar magnitude, suggesting that maximum efficacy is determined by the available number of peripheral opioid receptors rather than by the amount of agonist, in line with our previous observations after recruitment of opioid-producing inflammatory cells (Brack et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference from the data with citation to Brack et al., 2004.

claim: Upon local injection of morphine into inflamed paws, small amounts of morphine and a minor analgesic effect appeared in contralateral noninflamed paws, suggesting vascular absorption of morphine and subsequent stimulation of central opioid receptors.
source: Upon local injection of morphine into inflamed paws, small amounts of morphine and a minor analgesic effect appeared in contralateral noninflamed paws (Figure 6c), suggesting vascular absorption of morphine and subsequent stimulation of central opioid receptors.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral and microdialysis data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Concentrations of free morphine measured in brain, blood, and paw tissue corroborated the behavioral results showing differential effects of morphine vs. PG-M.
source: Concentrations of free morphine measured in brain, blood, and paw tissue corroborated these results.
evidence: This is a summary statement linking the concentration data to the behavioral data.

claim: The morphine levels in subcutaneous paw tissue within the first hour correlated well with analgesic actions.
source: Considering the low microdialysis perfusion rate (see below), the morphine levels in subcutaneous paw tissue within the first hour correlated well with analgesic actions, consistent with the notion that peripheral opioid receptors mediated these effects.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined microdialysis and behavioral data.

claim: Enhanced plasma extravasation most likely accounted for the higher morphine concentrations in inflamed than in noninflamed paws.
source: Enhanced plasma extravasation most likely accounted for the higher morphine concentrations in inflamed than in noninflamed paws.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed concentration differences.

claim: The conjugates are not cleaved in the absence of inflammation and are unable to cross the BBB.
source: This suggests that the conjugates are not cleaved in the absence of inflammation and are unable to cross the BBB.
evidence: This is an inference from the concentration data showing no free morphine in blood or brain after PG-M administration.

claim: After i.v. administration, PG-M is retained in the circulation, slowly accumulates at the target site and produces prolonged analgesia, likely based on the EPR effect.
source: Our data indicate that after i.v. administration, PG-M is retained in the circulation, slowly accumulates at the target site and produces prolonged analgesia, likely based on the EPR effect (Khandare et al., 2012; Azzopardi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the data with citations to studies on the EPR effect.

claim: After i.pl. administration, the analgesic effect was of shorter duration, consistent with the notion that PG-M does not need to extravasate and is cleaved soon after injection.
source: After i.pl. administration, the analgesic effect was of shorter duration, consistent with the notion that PG-M does not need to extravasate and is cleaved soon after injection.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data comparing i.v. and i.pl. administration.

claim: No free morphine was detectable in blood after i.v. PG-M, suggesting that this conjugate is stable in absence of leukocyte esterase at physiologic pH.
source: No free morphine was detectable in blood after i.v. PG-M, suggesting that this conjugate is stable in absence of leukocyte esterase at physiologic pH.
evidence: This is an inference from the blood concentration data.

claim: pH values of about 6.8 were measured in inflamed paws in vivo.
source: Our direct measurements revealed pH-values of about 6.8 in inflamed paws in vivo.
evidence: Supported by in vivo pH measurements.

claim: The combination of multiple inflammatory mediators and other lytic enzymes such as proteases may promote a much faster cleavage of PG-M in vivo than observed in vitro.
source: In addition to acidosis and leukocyte esterase, the combination of multiple inflammatory mediators and other lytic enzymes such as proteases may promote a much faster cleavage of PG-M in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between in vitro and in vivo release rates.

claim: These factors appear to contribute to the selective release of morphine from PG-M in injured but not in normal environment, as encountered in brain, blood, or intestinal wall.
source: These factors appear to contribute to the selective release of morphine from PG-M in injured but not in normal environment, as encountered in brain, blood, or intestinal wall.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: Microdialysis, locomotor, analgesia and binding assays clearly indicated that PG-M did not reach the CNS and did not bind to opioid receptors.
source: Indeed, while conventional morphine produced sedation both in the open field and in PPT experiments (rats receiving high doses frequently reached cut-off values), our microdialysis, locomotor, analgesia and binding assays clearly indicated that PG-M did not reach the CNS and did not bind to opioid receptors.
evidence: This is a summary inference from multiple types of experimental data.

claim: PG-M should not extravasate or be cleaved in the noninjured intestinal wall, consistent with the lack of constipation.
source: Consistent with the notion that PG-M should not extravasate or be cleaved in the noninjured intestinal wall, we did not detect any signs of constipation, in contrast to previously developed peripheral opioid agonists (e.g. loperamide).
evidence: This is an inference from the constipation data.

claim: Free hyperbranched PG has already been declared safe for in vivo application.
source: The abuse potential and organ toxicity of PG-M need to be investigated in further detail, although free hyperbranched PG has already been declared safe for in vivo application (Kainthan et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kainthan et al., 2006.

claim: PG-M may serve as prototype of a peripherally restricted opioid formulation designed to forego central and intestinal side effects.
source: Thus, PG-M may serve as prototype of a peripherally restricted opioid formulation designed to forego central and intestinal side effects.
evidence: This is a concluding inference from all the experimental data presented.

claim: The average molecular weight of PG-M was 21.4 kDa.
source: The average molecular weight of PG-M was 21.4 kDa.
evidence: Stated in the caption of Figure 5.

claim: The IC50 of PG-M for displacing [3H]-DAMGO from mu-opioid receptors was 18.7 ± 1.82 µM.
